title: NEB Class 11 Chemistry — Hydrocarbons — 2020
subject: chemistry
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: Explain the mechanism of the free-radical chlorination of methane in the presence of ultraviolet light, and account for the mixture of products formed.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Initiation (homolytic fission by UV light).**

$$\text{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} \text{Cl}^\bullet + \text{Cl}^\bullet$$

**Step 2 — Propagation.**

$$\text{Cl}^\bullet + \text{CH}_4 \rightarrow \text{HCl} + \text{CH}_3^\bullet$$

$$\text{CH}_3^\bullet + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{Cl} + \text{Cl}^\bullet$$

The chlorine radical is regenerated, so the chain continues.

**Step 3 — Termination.**

$$\text{Cl}^\bullet + \text{Cl}^\bullet \rightarrow \text{Cl}_2 \qquad \text{CH}_3^\bullet + \text{Cl}^\bullet \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{Cl} \qquad \text{CH}_3^\bullet + \text{CH}_3^\bullet \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_6$$

**Why a mixture forms.** The reaction is not selective: chlorine can attack any of the four equivalent C–H bonds of methane, and the process is highly random. A mixture of chloromethane, dichloromethane, chloroform and tetrachloromethane is obtained. Excess chlorine pushes the substitution further:

$$\text{CH}_4 + 4\text{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} \text{CCl}_4 + 4\text{HCl}$$
questions.knowledgeNote: Chlorination of methane is a chain radical reaction with initiation, propagation and termination steps, giving a statistical mixture of products.
questions.answer: **Free-radical chain mechanism (CH₄ + Cl₂ --UV--> CH₃Cl + HCl, then further substitution):** **Step 1 — initiation:** UV light homolyses Cl₂: Cl₂ --hν--> 2Cl• (two chlorine radicals). **Step 2 — propagation:** (a) Cl• abstracts H from methane: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + •CH₃; (b) the methyl radical attacks Cl₂: •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl• — the radical regenerated in (b) feeds step (a), so the chain continues thousands of cycles per initiation event. **Step 3 — termination:** radicals combine and the chain dies: Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂; •CH₃ + •CH₃ → CH₃–CH₃ (ethane by-product); •CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃Cl. **Why a mixture:** the product CH₃Cl is itself chlorinatable — Cl• abstracts its H too, giving CH₂Cl₂, then CHCl₃, then CCl₄; the reaction cannot 'stop' at monochloride because every product still has C–H bonds and the same radical machinery keeps working ⟹ a mixture of CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄ (plus ethane) results. Excess methane suppresses over-chlorination. **Deep point:** radical substitution is a chain reaction with no memory — each product re-enters as a substrate, and the mixture is the thermodynamic signature of a mechanism that cannot count.
